abstract: The Asiatic cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus), once widespread, now survives only in Iran, with its population nearing extinction. In this study, we synthesised 13 years (2012 to 2024) of monitoring data to assess demographic and spatial patterns of this critically endangered subspecies in Iran. Using extensive camera trap surveys across eight reserves, supplemented by published records of cheetah occurrences on social media, we identified 24 adult cheetahs in the Northern and Southern Landscapes. No reproduction or new individuals have been recorded in the Southern Landscape for over a decade, while the Northern Landscape supports the remaining population, likely fewer than 30 adult individuals. From 2012 to 2024, at least 38 cubs were born from eight females in the Northern Landscape, with 74.1% surviving their first year. The absence of any newly detected adults throughout the 13-year study period suggests that long-term individual-based monitoring has likely captured the entire known adult population. Asiatic cheetahs show high mobility, often crossing unprotected communal lands and a major highway, increasing mortality risks. Camera traps enabled us to effectively identify individuals but are limited for tracking fine-scale movements, underscoring the need for satellite telemetry. Roadside fencing, wildlife underpasses, habitat protection, community-based land management, and stronger anti-trafficking measures are critical to enhance survival. Genetic risks, including low population size and inbreeding, further threaten viability. These findings inform conservation strategies for endangered carnivores in arid ecosystems. Keywords: arid environment, camera trap, illegal wildlife trade, population viability, small population

summary: Thirteen years of camera-trap monitoring show Asiatic cheetahs in Iran number about 24 adults, with no reproduction in the Southern Landscape for a decade.
title: Will they survive? The critical status of Asiatic cheetahs in Iran
